doc.title: Branford Marsalis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Southern, Berklee and becoming a jazz player
title: Going to Berklee to write arrangements; MIDI and Wynton's Blakey gig
summary: He planned a Quincy Jones-style arranging career until MIDI threatened horn sections and Wynton joined Art Blakey.

bands.name: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well, I didn’t …I was…I didn’t have a conception of beauty. I was fifteen. Fifteen year olds don’t have any conception of beauty, man. They just don’t. I don’t know what it is. And, occasionally, Shostakovich did, when he was fifteen, but that’s…. That’s an isolated thing. It’s very unusual, very unusual. But, yeah they were nice solos. My dad was playing the records for me. But I learned a couple, just cause, you know, if you can’t do it, then you should try to do it…try to learn it. But it was still no idea…I just, you know…. When I went to Berklee, I went to go into production, like Quincy’s stuff, you know. Quincy Jones-type stuff. Writing arrangements, I was gonna move to L.A., write arrangements for the bands and do all the…. There was a guy named Tom Tom Eighty-four. It’s not his real name, but that’s what we called himself out of Chicago. And he was doing that stuff for Earth, Wind and Fire. And I said “Wow, I wanna do that.” And right around that time, MIDI showed up. I said, “Well, that’s it for the horn sections. (laughs) It was so clear that the horn sections were just going away. And I heard…Wynton had got the gig with Art Blakey and he was coming to town and I went to see that band. I didn’t go to hear it yet, but I did go to see it.
